newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Peabody says Mt Owen report "interesting".
newsitem.headline: Peabody says Mt Owen report "interesting".

text.p: Peabody Resources Ltd, owned by The Energy Group Plc, on Friday described as "interesting" a newspaper report which said The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd wanted to sell its Mount Owen mine.
Peabody managing director Robert Humphris declined to comment when asked if Peabody would bid for the thermal coal mine in the Hunter Valley region of New South Wales.
"I mean it (the report) is interesting," he told Reuters.
"You can almost postulate (that) up to 60 percent of the valley could be up for sale at the moment. That means only 40 percent are potential purchasers."
Earlier on Friday, The Australian Financial Review newspaper reported that BHP wanted to sell the Mount Owen open cut mine as part of a plan to quit the thermal coal market altogether.
The mine, commissioned eight months ago, has underperformed because of a difficult geological structure, the report said.
A BHP spokesman declined to comment on the report but said the company was reviewing all its coal assets, in line with a total review of the group's asset base.
BHP has also recently said that divestment of an asset would depend not only on its rate of return, but also whether it helps other, associated assets to deliver high returns.
BHP supplies its domestic steel-making operations with coking coal from its own mines, but thermal coal is exported.
Shell Australia Ltd, a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell group, has also said it wants to expands its presence in the Australian coal industry.
But on Friday Shell declined to say whether it would be interested in acquiring Mount Owen.
"We've got very, very good assets of our own at the moment anyway," a Shell spokeswoman said from Brisbane.

"I think what senior managers have indicated is that ultimately we will be looking for further prospects in Australia. It doesn't necessarily mean we could be acquiring anybody else's assets -- it could be -- but we also have exploration assets of our own going on."
The Hunter Valley coal-mining district is said to be ripe for buyers, with global miner Rio Tinto also casting a critical eye over its mines in the valley.
But Rio Tinto recently centralised management of its Hunter Valley mines, previously split between subsidiaries Coal and Allied and Novacoal. The group said it was in coal for the "long haul".
